101
Twenty Sixth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2008
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 24, pp 101-114
Validation of Air-Sea Interface Parameters in the
Southwest Indian Ocean Sector of the Southern
Ocean
Alvarinho J. Luis
National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research, Earth System Science
Organization, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Headland Sada, Goa
ABSTRACT
As a part of International Polar Year project, meteorological data from
NCEP-NCAR and ECMWF numerical weather forecasts (NWFs), QuikSCAT
winds and AMSR-E sea surface temperature (SST) in the surface atmospheric
boundary layer have been validated by using ship-based data collected in the
southwest Indian Ocean sector of the Southern Ocean during the 26
th Indian
Scientific Expedition to Antarctica. The NWFs overestimate mean sea level
pressure by –5 to –12 mb. The root mean square difference (rmsd) ranges from
1.7 to 2.3 mb and the regression yields a high correlation coefficient ( r)
exceeding 0.9, significant at 1% level. Validation of NWF air temperature yields
a rmsd of 0.8°C and r exceeding 0.9. Relative humidity from NWFs is
underestimated by 3%, and the data fail to capture sporadic events in the mid-
latitudes. The QuikSCAT winds are underestimates by 1.3 m s
–1 and show a
large bias south of 50°S. The validation of AMSR-E SST yields armsd of 0.7°C
and the correlation is highly significant ( r> 0.9). Validation of sensible and
latent heat fluxes from NWFs yields armsd in the range 17–19 and 38–42 Wm
–
2, respectively. The ECMWF heat fluxes are poorly correlated to the insitu data
than those from the NCEP-NCAR.
INTRODUCTION
Wind driven dynamics are crucial for a large scale heat exchange
between the ocean and atmosphere; for example, south of the Antarctic
Polar Front, approximately 300 PW of heat is lost to the atmosphere
(Keffer and Holloway, 1988). The physical processes in the Southern
Ocean (SO) are not well understood because it is under-surveyed by the
traditional observations due to its remoteness and inclement weather.
Though satellite observations and numerical weather forecasts are
available, their validation requires high-quality in-situdata. Under the
102
International Polar Year (IPY)–endorsed project (IPY#70) entitled
“Monitoring of the Upper Ocean Circulation, Transport and Water
Masses between Africa and Antarctica” (http://classic.ipy.org/development/
eoi/index.htm), hydrographic data are recorded during the 26th expedition.
This study is carried out by using the meteorological data collected by
using the ship’s automatic weather station.
OBJECTIVES
This paper addresses the analysis of meteorological data collected
during the 26 th ISEA on board MV Emerald Sea from Durban (32.4ºS,
30.4ºE) to India Bay, Antarctica (70.05°S, 12.45°E) during 9–14 February
2007 (Track–1) and from Prydz Bay, Antarctica (69.35°S, 76.17°E) to
Mauritius (20.15°S, 57.48°E) during 19–26 March 2007 (Track-2). In
particular, we elucidate large-scale meteorological features identified
along the two tracks, and validate the satellite and numerical weather
forecasts (NWF). Though the data points are few, it is hoped that this
work would help in understanding the extremes in the ABL conditions
in the SO and the validation would serve as one of the point of reference
India’s OCEANSAT–II mission scheduled to be launched in 2009 with
a Scatterometer for measuring ocean-surface wind and Ocean Color
Monitor for biophysical studies.
DATA AND METHODS
The ABL parameters, namely, wind speed (Ws), air temperatre
(Ta), relative humidity (Rh) and sea level pressure were recorded at
about three hourly interval from 32°S to the sea-ice edge at the
oceanographic station where Expendable bathythermograph (XBT) and
Expendable CTD (XCTD) profiles were obtained along Track–1 and –2
(Fig. 1). Ws was measured by using RM Young wind monitor with an
accuracy of ±0.3 ms
–1. Ta and Rh were recorded using PRT probe and
sensor equipped with capacitive polymer H-chip (make: Vaisala Inc.),
respectively; the accuracies of both these measurements are temperature
dependent. Digital barometer was used to record the atmospheric pressure
(make: Vaisala Inc., accuracy: ±0.3 hPa at 20°C), from which mean sea
level pressure (MSLP) was computed. Ws, Ta, and Rh were adjusted to
10 m height above the sea surface by using log-layer profiles (Liu et al.,
1979). Using these meteorological data and SST from XBT and XCTD,
sensible (Qs) and latent heat flux (Qe) were estimated by using bulk flux

algorithm (LKB; Liu et al., 1979). In this work, positive Qs and Qe
indicate surface heat loss to the atmosphere.
